title: Craft the job
hookLine: researchers found hospital cleaners who shaped their jobs around patients' care found more meaning (Wrzesniewski and Dutton, 2001)

lines: THE BLINDS, THE VISITOR, THE FLOORS.
cards: Two people clean the same hospital ward. Same mop, same pay, same list. One of them describes the job as cleaning rooms.
The other talks about the patients: which one likes the blinds open, which one hasn't had a visitor, how to time the floors so nobody is woken.

When researchers Amy Wrzesniewski and Jane Dutton looked at people like these, the second kind of cleaner saw the work as part of healing, and found more meaning in it. Nobody had rewritten their job description.
They had reshaped the job themselves. Today: job crafting.

teach.b: Wrzesniewski and Dutton called this job crafting: the ways people quietly reshape the work they've been given. Their paper describes three. First, the tasks.

You can add, drop or change what you do, or how you do it. The cleaner who times the floors so a patient can sleep has changed a task, without asking anyone. Second, the relationships: who you deal with, and how.
Some cleaners talked with patients and families, and saw themselves as part of the care team. The list never mentioned conversation; they added it.
Third, the way you see it. Cleaning rooms, or helping people heal: the work is identical, and the meaning isn't. Now a neighbor from much further back.
The poet and priest George Herbert wrote a short poem called The Elixir, about doing ordinary things for God.

One stanza says: "Who sweeps a room, as for thy laws, Makes that and th' action fine." For Herbert, the sweeping stays sweeping. What changes is what it's done for, and that changes both the room and the act.
The researchers don't speak of God, and Herbert didn't run a study.

They describe something that rhymes: the same task can be lifted by how it's held. Fourth, a caution. Job crafting isn't a way to excuse bad pay or bad bosses; some jobs need changing from the outside, too.
But inside a lot of work there's a little room to move, and that room is yours.

how: People who practice job crafting look for small changes within their role: adjusting a task, building a relationship, or reframing the work around the people it serves; some also hold their daily tasks as an offering, in the spirit of Herbert's poem.

o: rewriting your job description with your manager
making handmade crafts as a side job for extra pay
quietly reshaping the tasks and meaning of your job

games.q: three ways to craft a job — tap the pairs.
p: timing the floors so a patient sleeps
cleaning rooms, or helping people heal
who sweeps a room, as for thy laws

s: the cleaners who found more meaning had been given a different job description
the job description was the same; they reshaped the work themselves.
in Herbert's poem, sweeping becomes something other than sweeping
the sweeping stays sweeping; what changes is what it's done for.
job crafting can include changing how you see the work
the researchers describe tasks, relationships and the way you see the job.

games.q: you clean a hospital ward. a patient is asleep in the room you're supposed to mop next. what do you do?
o: mop it now; it's on the list.
do another room first and come back when they wake.
games.why: cleaners who crafted their jobs timed their work around patients' rest. the list didn't say to; they saw their work as part of the care.

practice: Hold your own work in mind, paid or unpaid, a job, a home, a study, a care you give, and breathe slowly. Picture one task you do often, one person your work touches, and what the work is for underneath the list.
Don't decide anything yet; just let one possibility rise, and hold it.

wordCard.voice: Job crafting. The ways people quietly reshape the tasks, relationships and meaning of the work they've been given. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: that room is yours. Same mop, same list, and still a different job. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Wrzesniewski and Dutton, "Crafting a Job: Revisioning Employees as Active Crafters of Their Work," Academy of Management Review (2001)
